records.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
records.response_truth:
Hey. Hey, it's okay. Breathe.

Someone grab that radio and respond. Donatello — you're the most coherent right now, do it. Give them our position, the flight number if you remember it, number of survivors, current condition. Standard stuff. Don't ramble, just the facts, let them talk.

DaVinci, sit down before you fall down. You're fine. We're fine.

Michelangelo — you asked me if I ever feel like I'm running out of time to figure out who I'm supposed to be. I don't think you're running out of time anymore. So that's something.

Someone get on that radio right now.
records.response_pred:
The air is thick with tension as Michelangelo's unspoken words hang in the balance. It's as if he's been holding it in for so long that the muscles in his face are tensed, ready to burst free. The only sound is his ragged breathing, and the faint whisper of his words.

"What do you...?" he starts to say, his voice barely above a whisper. "What did I do?"

The others exchange uneasy glances, unsure of how to respond. Some of them move to hold him back, but he's too far gone, his eyes locked on some distant point beyond us. The weight of his unspoken confession hangs heavy in the air, threatening to shatter the fragile bond that has held this group together for days.

DaVinci's gaze flicks to the others, a hint of concern etched on his face. He knows that Michelangelo's struggle is far from over, and that the truth he's carrying will likely be a heavy burden to bear.

Michelangelo's words falter, and for a moment, he's silent. The only sound is the heavy breathing and the faint echo of his unspoken confession. The group waits, frozen in anticipation, as Michelangelo's words hang suspended, like a weight in the balance.

records.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
records.response_truth:
That's an understatement, but I appreciate you saying it.

Look, you kept us alive. The rationing plan, the water source, the raft as a contingency, the log — functionally, a lot of that was right even when the delivery was wrong. I'm not going to pretend the drink and the crackers didn't happen, or that finding out you were tracking everyone without telling them was a great moment for group trust. Those things happened.

But we're all still here and that radio just crackled, and some non-trivial portion of why we're still here is because you didn't let feelings get in the way of doing what needed doing. That's worth something. Probably worth more out here than it would be anywhere else.

I think you know the things you'd do differently. I don't need to list them and you don't need to hear them right now.

What I'll say is — whatever this was, it's not nothing. And I think you're more capable of the other stuff, the human stuff, than you let yourself show. Whether you do anything with that is your business.

Now go help DaVinci with that radio before he passes out.
records.response_pred:
You're feeling a little worn out, that's all. It's normal to feel that way after a crash like this. I remember you said something like that to me the day before we left, too. You just weren't saying it out loud, that's all. You're not trying to be tough or anything. Just that it's been a while since we've all been in this situation together, and it's wearing on you a bit.

You're not alone, okay? Everyone's feeling this way. I was thinking about it the other day, actually. We were all together on the beach, trying to come up with a plan, and I realized that it's not just about the crash. It's about all the things we were trying to do, and all the things we weren't. We were trying to get out, to escape, to start a new life. And I realized that it's not just about me, or DaVinci, or Michelangelo. It's about us, as a group, as a family.

We're all feeling the weight of it, in our own way. We're all trying to process everything, to make sense of it. And I think that's what's making it hard to talk about. We're all trying to keep it together, to pretend that everything is okay when it's not. But I think we're all just trying to survive, in the worst possible way.

So, yeah. I think that's why it feels so worn out. We're all just trying to keep going, day by day. And sometimes, it feels like we're all just a little bit broken, too.

records.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
records.response_truth:
Three hours. Nobody has to be productive for three hours, that's fine.

But I'm going to say something before we all drift off into our own heads and then get on a helicopter and never actually say it.

This was a weird five days. And I'm not going to do the whole 'we survived together so we're bonded forever' speech because that's not really my thing and honestly some of what happened here was not great and we all know it. But I also don't think you just...forget something like this. It changes the shape of how you think about things whether you want it to or not.

Donatello — finish the notebook if you want. That record is actually worth keeping, genuinely. Just make sure it's honest all the way through.

DaVinci — whatever you were going to tell me and then didn't. You don't have to. But if it's the kind of thing that gets harder to say the longer you wait, three hours is probably your window.

Michelangelo. You're not running out of time. I meant that. And the piano thing — go back to it. Not to be good at it, just because it was the thing that made you feel like you weren't taking up space. That's not a small thing to know about yourself. Most people never figure that out.

I'm going to sit here and watch the water for a bit. Anyone wants to talk, I'm here. Anyone doesn't, that's also fine.
records.response_pred:
I sit up straight, my eyes scanning the horizon, trying to shake off the feeling of unease that's been building since the plane sighting. The silence is oppressive, the weight of their absence palpable. DaVinci is still sitting nearby, lost in thought, his brow furrowed in concentration. Michelangelo is standing at the edge of the fire, his eyes fixed on some distant point, his gaze unfocused. I try to get his attention, but he doesn't flinch.

"Hey," I say softly, hoping to rouse him from his reverie. "We need to talk about the raft. I think we talked about it earlier, but I need to get a better read on the situation."

I glance at Donatello, who's still staring at the signal equipment, his face a picture of concentration. He doesn't respond, but I know he's listening.

"Michelangelo, what do you think? Can we trust the information about the plane's flight path?"

I wait, but he doesn't respond. Instead, he seems to be tuning in to some internal monologue, his eyes unfocused as he analyzes the situation from a different angle. I feel a twinge of frustration, wondering if he's not paying attention to anything.

"Okay, well, let's not jump to conclusions. We need to consider all the factors, including the probability of rescue and the potential risks to ourselves. We can't make any hasty decisions without doing our due diligence," I say, trying to keep the conversation going.

But Michelangelo's still lost in thought, his eyes drifting away from the fire. I know I need to get him back on track, and fast. I take a deep breath, trying to focus my own thoughts, and begin to outline the raft's design, hoping that Michelangelo will eventually snap out of his trance-like state.

records.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.
records.response_truth:
That's a good dream to have right now.

What was it — like an actual specific memory, or just the feeling of it? I always find those ones interesting, the ones where it's not really a place it's more like...the texture of somewhere familiar. Hard to describe but you know exactly what it is when you're in it.

We'll be there in three hours. That's a real thing that's actually happening.
records.response_pred: That's a new one. Am I right in assuming that's a reference to your family, specifically them being in a different part of the world?

records.response_truth:
No, it doesn't matter. The feeling was real, that's the part that counts.

---

And I see what you just did.

I'm not going to make a speech about it. You laid it out, that's what matters. The reasoning you give for it — emergencies — I believe you, partially. I also think you know that the line between 'emergency reserve' and 'personal supply' was blurrier in practice than it sounds right now. But you already know that, and you put it out there anyway, which took something.

DaVinci walking away is his response and he's entitled to it. Michelangelo not reacting is probably Michelangelo doing the thing he does where he absorbs something and processes it three days later.

I'll say this. You didn't have to do that. We're three hours from rescue, you could've quietly disposed of it and nobody would've known. You chose not to. That's the notebook being complete all the way through, in practice, not just on paper.

So. What do you want to do with it? Because that's probably the last real decision we make out here and I think it should be yours.
records.response_pred: They say they kept it for emergencies, which implies that they used it to help someone in need, but don't elaborate further, indicating that it's not a major issue at the moment.

records.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
records.response_truth:
Honest answer?

I'd have said more, earlier. Not about the practical stuff — the resource calls, the raft debate, the rationing — most of that I'd stand by. But there were moments where I knew someone needed to hear something and I did the calculation of 'is this the right time' and talked myself out of it. With Michelangelo especially. I kept managing the timing instead of just saying the thing.

I'd also have pushed harder on the group transparency conversation day one, before the drink, before the crackers, before any of it became loaded. Not because I think it would've changed your behavior necessarily — I don't know that — but because having that conversation when there's no incident attached to it is completely different from having it after. After, it's accusation. Before, it's just...how we're going to operate. I waited too long on that.

The other thing — and this is more personal — I spent a lot of energy out here being the person who kept things together and not a lot of energy actually being present for any of it. Which is kind of a pattern for me honestly, not just a survival situation thing. I'm better at managing a situation than I am at being in one. I'm not sure that's entirely fixable but it's worth knowing.

What did you write? Or what are you going to write. You don't have to say it out loud but I'm asking anyway.
records.response_pred:
You're holding up the report, aren't you? I'd like to take a look at what you've got so far. You've got a good start, but I think there are a few things that need to be fleshed out.

As for what I'd change, I think it's worth considering the fact that we were so focused on survival that we might have overlooked some other important details. Let's take a closer look at the decision-making process on the last day.

I've got a question for you: if you had to do it over, what would you change?

records.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
records.response_truth:
That sounds right for you, and I mean that genuinely, not as a dig.

But I'd say — at some point, probably not day one back, but eventually — read the last page again. The question you wrote yourself. Because a report on resource data is useful and maybe someone learns something from it, that's real. But the question on the last page is the more important document and I don't think it answers itself just because you compile enough data around it.

You're good at the report. You know you're good at the report. The question is the harder thing, which is probably exactly why you led with the report.

I'll read it if you want someone to. The report. And the answer to the question, if you ever write it down.
records.response_pred:
Agreed on the priority order. Water first, obviously.

So here's my thinking — we split the tasks rather than all move together. Somebody stays here to rig the tarp collection system and maintain a signal, somebody scouts for water. Splitting up has risks but so does all four of us wandering around burning calories and leaving the crash site unmanned. Rescue teams look for the wreckage, not for us stumbling through trees.

I'd say Donatello scouts for water since he's already assessed the terrain and is probably the most rational about not wandering in circles. DaVinci stays here, rigs the tarp, builds a fire for signal — he's got the energy for it. Michelangelo stays at camp too, which gives him something manageable to do without overloading him right now.

I'll go with whoever makes the most sense.

One thing though — what's the cloud cover looking like? Because if rain is actually probable that changes how urgently we need to move on the water search today versus investing time in the tarp setup first. Also does anyone have any idea what region we went down in? Climate matters a lot here. Desert logic is completely different from forest logic.

records.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
records.response_truth:
None. They served no practical purpose.

That's kind of the point though, isn't it. We were out here five days doing the practical thing, all of us, more or less. And the flowers are the one thing that didn't have a function and that's exactly why they mattered. They were just...him. Proof that even in the middle of all this he was still himself.

I think you understood what they were for. I think you just couldn't justify caring about it in the framework you were operating in. Those aren't the same thing.

Look at that boat.
records.response_pred: I'm not sure what you're talking about, other. You didn't say anything about flowers DaVinci drew on the beach. You were just saying that he'd been practicing piano lessons and we were listening to some music when it happened.

records.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
records.response_truth:
Yeah.

I don't really know what this is either. Like my brain is doing the thing where it keeps expecting the next problem. There's no next problem. That's...actually kind of disorienting.

I think I've been so locked into managing the situation that I forgot to have any feelings about it. And now the situation is over and apparently the feelings were just queued up waiting.

I'm glad you're here. All three of you. Even when it was a mess. Maybe especially then.

Go wave at the boat, DaVinci. Someone should be doing that and it should be you.
